title: Àwọn ìṣe̩ tí a tí ṣe̩ / Talking about past experiences
bridge: In English, past experiences are often expressed with the simple past tense ('I went', 'I saw') or present perfect ('I have been'). Yoruba, however, uses the perfective aspect marker 'tí' (or 'tí') to indicate completed actions, which functions differently from English. Unlike English, Yoruba does not distinguish between simple past and present perfect in the same way. For example, 'I have eaten' and 'I ate' can both translate to 'Mo ti je̩un' in Yoruba, relying on context. A common trap is overusing English past tense structures in Yoruba, which can sound unnatural or incorrect.
rule: In Yoruba, to talk about past experiences, use the perfective aspect marker 'tí' (or 'tí' before vowels) before the verb. The structure is: Subject + tí + verb (past participle form). For negative sentences, use 'kò tí' instead of 'tí'. For questions, use 'ṣe̩' at the beginning or 'tí' at the end. The verb does not change form based on tense; context and the marker 'tí' indicate the past. Note that 'tí' can also mean 'that' in other contexts, so pay attention to sentence structure. Examples: 'Mo tí lòdé' (I have gone to the market), 'Kò tí je̩un' (He/She has not eaten), 'Ṣe̩ o tí wòn?' (Have you seen them?).

concept_examples.translation: I went to the market yesterday.

concept_examples.text: Ẹ̀mi tí wọ́n kò tí gbọ́.
concept_examples.phonetic: ɛ̀mī tī́ wɔ́n kò tī́ gbɔ́.

concept_examples.text: Àwọn ọkùnrin tí wọ́n tí ṣe̩ ìṣẹ́ yìí.
concept_examples.translation: The men have done this work.
concept_examples.phonetic: àwɔ̀n ɔ̀kùnrīn tī́ wɔ́n tī́ ṣḗ ìṣɛ́ yìí.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often omit the perfective marker 'tí' when translating past actions directly from English. In Yoruba, 'tí' is required to indicate that the action is completed in the past. Without 'tí', the sentence sounds incomplete or incorrect to native speakers.

examples.original: Mo tí je̩un lọ́là.
examples.phonetic: mō tī́ jḗūn lɔ́là.
examples.translation: I ate yesterday.
examples.note: Introduces the basic structure with 'tí' + verb for a single past action.

examples.original: Wọ́n tí lòdọ̀ ọkọ̀.
examples.phonetic: wɔ́n tī́ lōdɔ̀ ọ̀kɔ̀.
examples.translation: They traveled by car.
examples.note: Demonstrates the marker 'tí' with different verbs and objects.

examples.original: Ẹ̀mi tí mo tí fẹ́.
examples.phonetic: ɛ̀mī tī́ mō tī́ fɛ́.
examples.translation: The thing I wanted.
examples.note: Shows 'tí' used in relative clauses to indicate past action.

examples.original: Kò tí gbọ́.
examples.phonetic: kò tī́ gbɔ́.
examples.translation: He/She didn’t hear.
examples.note: Introduces the negative form 'kò tí' for past actions.

examples.original: Mo tí lòdé, tí je̩un, tí wá ilé.
examples.phonetic: mō tī́ lṑdḗ, tī́ jḗūn, tī́ wá ilé.
examples.translation: I went to the market, ate, and came home.
examples.note: Combines multiple past actions using 'tí' before each verb.

examples.original: Wọ́n tí gbọ́, tí fẹ́, tí ṣe̩ ìṣẹ́.
examples.phonetic: wɔ́n tī́ gbɔ́, tī́ fɛ́, tī́ ṣḗ ìṣɛ́.
examples.translation: They heard, wanted, and did the work.
examples.note: Shows sequential past actions with 'tí'.

examples.original: Mo tí wòn ní ìlú, tí wọ́n tí ṣe̩ ìṣẹ́.
examples.phonetic: mō tī́ wɔ̀n ní ìlú, tī́ wɔ́n tī́ ṣḗ ìṣɛ́.
examples.translation: I saw them in the city, and they had done the work.
examples.note: Demonstrates past actions with additional context.

examples.original: Kò tí wòn, kò tí gbọ́.
examples.phonetic: kò tī́ wɔ̀n, kò tī́ gbɔ́.
examples.translation: They didn’t see, and they didn’t hear.
examples.note: Negative form for multiple past actions.

examples.original: Mo tí lòdé lọ́là, tí je̩un ní ọ̀sẹ̀.
examples.phonetic: mō tī́ lṑdḗ lɔ́là, tī́ jḗūn ní ɔ̀sɛ̀.
examples.translation: I went to the market yesterday, and ate on Sunday.
examples.note: Combines past actions with specific time expressions like 'lọ́là' and 'ní ọ̀sẹ̀'.

examples.original: Wọ́n tí ṣe̩ ìṣẹ́ ní ọjọ́ mẹ́ta.
examples.phonetic: wɔ́n tī́ ṣḗ ìṣɛ́ ní ɔ̀jɔ́ mɛ́tà.
examples.translation: They did the work for three days.
examples.note: Uses time expressions to specify duration or frequency.

examples.original: Mo tí wòn ní ìlú Ìbàdàn lọ́là.
examples.phonetic: mō tī́ wɔ̀n ní ìlú Ìbàdàn lɔ́là.
examples.translation: I saw them in Ibadan yesterday.
examples.note: Includes location and time in past action sentences.

examples.original: Kò tí gbọ́ ní ọjọ́ mẹ́rin.
examples.phonetic: kò tī́ gbɔ́ ní ɔ̀jɔ́ mɛ́rīn.
examples.translation: He/She didn’t hear for four days.
examples.note: Negative past action with time expression.

title: Ṣe àwọn ìtọ́jú àwọn ìtẹ́lẹ̀ / Making plans and arrangements
bridge: In English, making plans often relies on modal verbs like 'can', 'will', or 'shall' (e.g., 'Can we meet tomorrow?'). Yoruba, however, uses a combination of the verb 'ṣe' (to do/make) with the infinitive form of the main verb (e.g., 'Ṣe àwọn ó lè jọ̀wọ́ jọ̀wọ́ lọ́dọ̀n mì?' = 'Can we meet tomorrow?'). English speakers might mistakenly use direct translations of 'can' or 'will' without the 'ṣe' structure, leading to unnatural phrasing. Additionally, Yoruba often omits explicit subjects when the context is clear, unlike English, which requires them.
rule: To make plans in Yoruba at A2 level, use the structure: 'Ṣe [subject] + lè + infinitive verb + [time/place]?' to ask for permission or ability to do something. The infinitive verb is formed by adding '-n' or '-ṣe' to the verb stem (e.g., 'jọ̀' + '-wọ́' = 'jọ̀wọ́' for 'meet'). For arrangements, use 'Jọ̀wọ́ + [subject] + infinitive verb + [time/place]' to suggest or request. The verb 'lè' (can) is often used in questions, while 'ma' (don't) + infinitive can soften requests (e.g., 'Ma jọ̀wọ́ lọ́dọ̀n mì' = 'Don't meet me tomorrow'). Time phrases typically follow the verb (e.g., 'lọ́dọ̀n mì' = tomorrow).

concept_examples.text: Ṣe àwọn ó lè jọ̀wọ́ lọ́dọ̀n mì?
concept_examples.phonetic: ʃe à.wɔ̃ lé lè dʒɔ̀.wɔ́ lɔ́.dɔ̃̀ mì?

concept_examples.text: Jọ̀wọ́ ẹ jọ̀wọ́ ní ìbùkún fún mi ní ọjọ́ kejì.
concept_examples.translation: Please meet me at the park on Wednesday.
concept_examples.phonetic: dʒɔ̀.wɔ́ ɛ̄ dʒɔ̀.wɔ́ ní ì.bù.kú̃ fú̃ mí ní ɔ̀.dʒɔ́ kɛ̀.dʒì.

concept_examples.text: Ṣe àwọn ó lè wá ní ọjọ́ kẹ́ta?
concept_examples.phonetic: ʃe à.wɔ̃ lé lè wá ní ɔ̀.dʒɔ́ kɛ́.tà?

concept_examples.text: Ma jọ̀wọ́ lọ́dọ̀n mì, ṣugbọn jọ̀wọ́ lọ́dọ̀n ọjọ́ kejì.
concept_examples.translation: Don't meet me tomorrow, but please meet on Wednesday.
concept_examples.phonetic: mà dʒɔ̀.wɔ́ lɔ́.dɔ̃̀ mì, ʃu.gbɔ̃̀ dʒɔ̀.wɔ́ lɔ́.dɔ̃̀ ọ̀.dʒɔ́ kɛ̀.dʒì.

common_error.correct: Ṣe àwọn ó lè jọ̀wọ́ lọ́dọ̀n mì?
common_error.explanation: English speakers often translate 'Can we meet tomorrow?' directly as 'A ṣe àwọn lè jọ̀wọ́ lọ́dọ̀n mì?' which is unnatural. The correct structure uses 'Ṣe' + subject + 'lè' + infinitive verb for questions about ability or permission. Alternatively, 'Jọ̀wọ́' + subject + infinitive can be used for direct requests. The verb 'lè' is crucial in questions to indicate possibility.

examples.original: Ṣe àwọn ó lè wá ní ọjọ́ kejì?
examples.phonetic: ʃe à.wɔ̃ lé lè wá ní ɔ̀.dʒɔ́ kɛ̀.dʒì?

examples.note: Introduces the basic question structure with 'lè' for ability or permission.

examples.original: Ṣe ẹ lè jọ̀wọ́ ní ilé mi ní ọjọ́ kẹ́ta?

examples.note: Practices asking for permission with location phrases.

examples.original: Ṣe àwọn a lè ṣe àwọn ọjọ́ mọ́?
examples.phonetic: ʃe à.wɔ̃ à lè ʃe à.wɔ̃ ɔ̀.dʒɔ́ mɔ́?
examples.translation: Can we do it another day?
examples.note: Introduces flexibility in planning with 'mọ́' (another).

examples.original: Ṣe ẹ lè wá ní ọjọ́ kẹ́ta?
examples.phonetic: ʃe ɛ̄ lé lè wá ní ɔ̀.dʒọ́ kɛ́.tà?
examples.translation: Can you come on Friday?
examples.note: Focuses on the verb 'wá' (to come) in planning contexts.

examples.phonetic: dʒɔ̀.wɔ́ ɛ̄ dʒɔ̀.wɔ́ ní í.lé mí ní ɔ̀.dʒɔ́ kɛ̀.dʒì?
examples.translation: Please meet me at my house on Wednesday.
examples.note: Introduces direct requests using 'Jọ̀wọ́' + subject + infinitive.

examples.original: Ma jọ̀wọ́ lọ́dọ̀n mì, ṣugbọn jọ̀wọ́ lọ́dọ̀n ọjọ́ kejì.

examples.translation: Don't meet me tomorrow, but please meet on Wednesday.
examples.note: Practices softening requests with 'Ma' + infinitive to avoid direct refusal.

examples.original: Jọ̀wọ́ àwọn wá ní ọjọ́ kẹ́ta.
examples.phonetic: dʒɔ̀.wɔ́ à.wɔ̃ wá ní ɔ̀.dʒɔ́ kɛ́.tà?
examples.translation: Please come on Friday.
examples.note: Focuses on the verb 'wá' (to come) in polite requests.

examples.original: Jọ̀wọ́ ẹ ṣe àwọn ọjọ́ mọ́.
examples.phonetic: dʒɔ̀.wɔ́ ɛ̄ ʃe à.wɔ̃ ɔ̀.dʒɔ́ mɔ́?
examples.translation: Please do it another day.
examples.note: Introduces the verb 'ṣe' (to do/make) in flexible planning.

examples.original: Jọ̀wọ́ àwọn jọ̀wọ́ ní ọjọ́ kẹ́ta ní ilé mi.
examples.phonetic: dʒɔ̀.wɔ́ à.wɔ̃ dʒɔ̀.wɔ́ ní ɔ̀.dʒɔ́ kɛ́.tà ní í.lé mí?
examples.translation: Please meet on Friday at my house.
examples.note: Combines time ('ọjọ́ kẹ́ta') and place ('ní ilé mi') in a request.

examples.original: Ṣe àwọn ó lè wá ní ọjọ́ kejì ní ilé ẹ̀kọ́?
examples.phonetic: ʃe à.wɔ̃ lé lè wá ní ɔ̀.dʒɔ́ kɛ̀.dʒì ní í.lé ɛ̀.kɔ́?
examples.translation: Can they come to school on Wednesday?
examples.note: Practices asking about specific locations with 'ní'.

examples.original: Ma jọ̀wọ́ lọ́dọ̀n mì, ṣugbọn jọ̀wọ́ lọ́dọ̀n ọjọ́ kejì ní ilé ẹ̀kọ́.
examples.phonetic: mà dʒɔ̀.wɔ́ lɔ́.dɔ̃̀ mì, ʃu.gbɔ̃̀ dʒɔ̀.wɔ́ lɔ́.dɔ̃̀ ọ̀.dʒɔ́ kɛ̀.dʒì ní í.lé ɛ̀.kɔ́?
examples.translation: Don't meet me tomorrow, but please meet at school on Wednesday.
examples.note: Combines negation ('Ma'), time, and place in a single sentence.

examples.original: Jọ̀wọ́ àwọn wá ní ọjọ́ mọ́ ní ilé mi.
examples.phonetic: dʒ̀.wɔ́ à.wɔ̃ wá ní ɔ̀.dʒɔ́ mɔ́ ní í.lé mí?
examples.translation: Please come another day to my house.
examples.note: Practices using 'mọ́' (another) with time and place in requests.

title: Ṣe àwọn àdàkú àti àwọn ìtọ́jú / Giving advice and recommendations
bridge: In English, advice is often given using modal verbs like 'should,' 'ought to,' or 'had better,' which are straightforward for learners. However, in Yoruba, advice is typically structured using the verb suffix '-kú' (meaning 'to do something thoroughly or persistently') or the phrase 'kí o...' (meaning 'you should...'). Unlike English, Yoruba does not use modal verbs in the same way, and the tone of advice can sound more direct or imperative. Learners may mistakenly transfer English structures like 'You should go' as 'O máa lo' (which literally means 'You will go') instead of the correct 'Kí o lo' or 'Ẹ lo'.
rule:
In Yoruba, advice and recommendations are commonly formed using:
1. The imperative structure 'Kí o...' (You should...) for polite advice:
   - Kí o + verb (present tense) + (object)
   - Example: Kí o jeun (You should eat).
   - Negative form: Kí o máa + verb (present tense) + (object)
     Example: Kí o máa jeun (You should not eat).

2. The suffix '-kú' to emphasize thoroughness or persistence:
   - Verb + '-kú' + (object)
   - Example: Jẹ́kú (Eat thoroughly/keep eating).
   - This is more forceful and less common for general advice but can be used for strong recommendations.

3. The phrase 'Ẹ...' (You all/Let's...) for group advice:
   - Ẹ + verb (present tense) + (object)
   - Example: Ẹ lo (You all go).

Key exceptions:
- For negative advice, use 'Kí o máa...' or 'Ẹ máa...' instead of 'Kí o...' + negative verb.
- The suffix '-kú' is not used with all verbs; it is more common with action verbs like 'je' (eat), 'lo' (go), or 'wọ̀' (wear).
- In some contexts, advice can also be given using 'Ẹ ṣe...' (You should do...), which is more formal.

concept_examples.text: Kí o máa lo sí ilé-ìwé ní ààyọ̀.
concept_examples.translation: You should go to school in the morning.
concept_examples.phonetic: kí ó máa ló sílé-ìwé ní àà-ìyọ̀

concept_examples.text: Ẹ jẹ́kú àwọn ẹbà tí a fún yín.
concept_examples.translation: You all should eat the food that was given to you.
concept_examples.phonetic: ɛ́ jɛ́kú àwɔ̀n ɛ̀bà tí à fún yín

concept_examples.text: Kí o wọ̀ àwọn ẹ̀kú́ àti àwọn ìrókò̀.
concept_examples.translation: You should wear the shoes and the hat.
concept_examples.phonetic: kí ó wɔ̀ àwɔ̀n ɛ̀kú́ àti àwɔ̀n ìrókò̀

concept_examples.text: Ẹ máa ṣe àwọn ìṣẹ́ tí a fún yín ní ìpàdé.
concept_examples.translation: You all should do the tasks that were given to you at the meeting.
concept_examples.phonetic: ɛ́ máa ṣɛ́ àwɔ̀n ìṣɛ́ tí à fún yín ní ìpàdé

common_error.wrong: O máa lo sí ilé-ìwé ní ààyọ̀.
common_error.correct: Kí o máa lo sí ilé-ìwé ní ààyọ̀.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often translate 'You should go' directly as 'O máa lo' (You will go), which is incorrect for giving advice. In Yoruba, 'O máa lo' implies a future action rather than a recommendation. The correct structure uses 'Kí o...' to convey advice or a suggestion. The phrase 'Kí o...' is essential for polite advice in Yoruba.

examples.original: Kí o máa jeun ní àárọ̀.
examples.phonetic: kí ó máa jɛ́un ní àà-rɔ̀
examples.translation: You should eat in the morning.
examples.note: Introduces the basic structure for giving advice using 'Kí o máa...' for negative advice.

examples.original: Kí o lo sí ìlú.
examples.phonetic: kí ó ló sí ìlú
examples.translation: You should go to the city.
examples.note: Highlights the use of 'Kí o...' for positive advice without negation.

examples.original: Kí o máa wọ̀ àwọn ẹ̀kú́.
examples.phonetic: kí ó máa wɔ̀ àwɔ̀n ɛ̀kú́
examples.translation: You should not wear those shoes.
examples.note: Demonstrates the negative form 'Kí o máa...' for advice.

examples.original: Kí o ṣe àwọn ìṣẹ́ yẹn.
examples.phonetic: kí ó ṣɛ́ àwɔ̀n ìṣɛ́ yɛ̀n
examples.translation: You should do those tasks.
examples.note: Shows the use of 'Kí o...' with verbs other than motion or eating.

examples.original: Ẹ lo sí ìlú ní ààyọ̀.
examples.phonetic: ɛ́ ló sí ìlú ní àà-yọ̀
examples.translation: You all should go to the city in the morning.
examples.note: Introduces the use of 'Ẹ...' for giving advice to a group.

examples.original: Ẹ máa jeun pẹ̀lú wa.
examples.phonetic: ɛ́ máa jɛ́un pɛ̀lú wà
examples.translation: You all should eat with us.
examples.note: Demonstrates the negative form 'Ẹ máa...' for group advice.

examples.original: Ẹ ṣe àwọn ìṣẹ́ yẹn ní ìpàdé.
examples.phonetic: ɛ́ ṣɛ́ àwɔ̀n ìṣɛ́ yɛ̀n ní ìpàdé
examples.translation: You all should do those tasks at the meeting.
examples.note: Shows the use of 'Ẹ...' with verbs other than motion or eating.

examples.original: Ẹ wọ̀ àwọn ẹ̀kú́ yẹn.
examples.phonetic: ɛ́ wɔ̀ àwɔ̀n ɛ̀kú́ yɛ̀n
examples.translation: You all should wear those shoes.
examples.note: Highlights the use of 'Ẹ...' for group advice with clothing.

examples.original: Jẹ́kú àwọn ẹbà tí a fún yín.
examples.phonetic: dʒɛ́kú àwɔ̀n ɛ̀bà tí à fún yín
examples.translation: Eat thoroughly the food that was given to you.
examples.note: Introduces the suffix '-kú' to emphasize thoroughness or persistence in advice.

examples.original: Lo kú sí ilé-ìwé ní ààyọ̀.
examples.phonetic: lɔ́ kú sí ilé-ìwé ní àà-yọ̀
examples.translation: Go thoroughly to school in the morning.
examples.note: Demonstrates the use of '-kú' with motion verbs for strong recommendations.

examples.original: Wọ̀ kú àwọn ẹ̀kú́ yẹn.
examples.phonetic: wɔ̀ kú àwɔ̀n ɛ̀kú́ yɛ̀n
examples.translation: Wear thoroughly those shoes.
examples.note: Shows the use of '-kú' with clothing verbs for strong advice.

examples.original: Ṣe kú àwọn ìṣẹ́ yẹn.
examples.phonetic: ʃɛ́ kú àwɔ̀n ìṣɛ́ yɛ̀n
examples.translation: Do thoroughly those tasks.
